claims.claimText: The University of Sydney's current student guidance (last updated 2 June 2026) says students can use AI in open (unsupervised) assessments, where educators guide the appropriate types of use and AI use must be acknowledged, but generally cannot use AI in secure (supervised) assessments unless the unit coordinator has given express permission in the unit outline. Each unit outline has a 'Use of AI' column showing, per assessment, AI prohibited, AI allowed, AI limited, or not applicable. This replaces the earlier Semester 1 2025 transition wording.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Your unit outline includes a "Use of AI" column to indicate whether you can use AI or not for each assessment.
evidence.snippetLocation: Unit of study outlines; lines 39-39 of captured page text

claims.claimText: University of Sydney guidance states that misusing AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy, with examples including submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment, using AI where it has been prohibited in a secure assessment such as a secure exam, and inputting University teaching or course materials, other students' content, external partners' intellectual property or any person's personal or health information. Citing non-existent references because AI output was not verified is not acceptable and risks an academic integrity breach.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
Misusing AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy. Examples of misuse include:
Submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment
using AI where it has been prohibited in a ‘secure’ assessment type, such as during a secure exam
inputting University teaching or course materials, content generated by another student, intellectual property from external partners, or any person’s personal or health information.
evidence.snippetLocation: Misuse of AI; lines 71-77 of captured page text

claims.claimText: If University of Sydney students use AI in assessments they must acknowledge it, including generative AI translation, paraphrasing or referencing tools; tools used only for word processing or basic spelling and grammar correction need not be acknowledged. Where permitted by the unit outline, the statement must say that AI tools were used and give the tool's name and version, the publisher, the URL and a brief description of how it was used; unit coordinators may add requirements such as a log of AI inputs and outputs.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: If you use AI in your assessments, you're required to acknowledge it – this includes acknowledging any tools that use generative AI, such as translation tools, paraphrasing tools or referencing tools. You are not required to acknowledge tools used for word processing, or which only correct basic spelling and grammar.
evidence.snippetLocation: Acknowledging AI use; lines 89-89 of captured page text

claims.claimText: Higher degree by research (HDR) students at the University of Sydney do not inherit the open-assessment AI permission. The Graduate Research guidance says generative AI may in general be used to improve spelling or grammar (spelling/grammar checkers and reference managers are permitted) but not to generate content; prompting AI to generate written or other content, uploading a draft to improve its academic language, and incorporating AI outputs as substantive thesis content are prohibited, except where AI is integral to the research design or methodology and approved by the supervisor and through the ethics arrangements. HDR students should never enter personal, sensitive or confidential information into any gen AI tool.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: In general terms, gen AI tools may be used where, for example, they assist in improving the spelling or grammar of your writing, but not where they generate content for you.
evidence.snippetLocation: Use of generative AI: General overview; lines 316-316 of captured page text

claims.claimText: University of Sydney academic decisions and misconduct findings use different review routes. For academic decisions, students may apply for faculty or Academic Panel review within 20 working days, and may appeal to the Student Appeals Body (SAB) within 15 working days of the review outcome, but not simply because they disagree with it. Where the Registrar makes a misconduct finding or penalty, the student may appeal to the Student Disciplinary Appeals Committee (SDAC) within 20 working days of the penalty notice. Not every AI-related academic integrity matter is a Registrar misconduct decision.

claims.claimText: At the University of Sydney, minor academic integrity breaches may be handled locally by unit coordinators, more serious ones are investigated by the faculty Educational Integrity team, and the most serious suspected cheating is handled by the Registrar under the Student Discipline Rule. claims.claimText: Besides Copilot, the University of Sydney lists Cogniti (designed by University educators), Harvey AI (available to all Sydney Law School students, a faculty-specific legal tool) and ChatGPT Edu. ChatGPT Edu is not yet available to all students: a student pilot is planned for October 2026 and release to all students is scheduled for Semester 1 2027. Custom GPTs, agents, plugins and connectors are individually assessed before being enabled. Its data are stored in Australia at rest, with globally routed inference.
